prompt: What is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto?

answer:

**General Requirements:**
- Must be a self-contained residential unit on the same lot as a detached house, semi-detached house, or townhouse, generally located in the rear yard next to a laneway [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

- Alternative compliance options exist for travel distances up to 90 metres with additional mitigating features like sprinkler systems [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2020/ph/bgrd/backgroundfile-156421.pdf]

**Required Documentation:**
- Site plan showing property lines, existing/proposed buildings, setbacks, parking areas, etc.
- Lot grading plan
- Floor plans for each level
- Roof plan
- Truss drawings and floor joist plan (if engineered systems are used)
- Elevations
- Cross sections
- Construction details and notes

- Energy Efficiency Design Summary form
- Municipal Road Damage form
- Schedule 1: Designer Information form
- Tree Declaration form (if trees may be affected)
- Plumbing Data Sheet (if plumbing work is included)

All documents must be in PDF format, drawn to scale, fully dimensioned, and signed/dated by qualified designers where applicable [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

*   **Fee:** $20.02 for every $1,000 of construction value. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/9678-1184441-c.pdf]

prompt: What inspections are required during construction in Toronto?
answer:
Building inspections are required at each critical stage of construction in Toronto, as per the Ontario Building Code, Subsection 1.3.5.1. The specific inspections required for your particular project can be confirmed by a Building Inspector. The following are examples of inspections that may be required:

For small buildings (Part 9 of the Ontario Building Code including houses and small commercial structures):

* Footing formwork and reinforcing steel before placing concrete
* Foundation wall formwork and reinforcing steel before placing concrete
* Damp proofing and draintile before backfilling
* Roughed-in plumbing
* Framing (prior to insulation)
* Insulation, vapour/air barrier and drywall/finished ceiling
* Final inspections upon completion of the project

For large buildings (Part 3 of the Ontario Building Code):

* Excavation and footings before placing concrete
* Foundation walls
* Damp proofing and draintile
* Backfilling and grade
* Framing, masonry, and roofing
* Fire protection, firestopping
* Plumbing, mechanical, electrical
* Insulation, vapor/air barrier, drywall/finish
* Final inspections upon completion of the project

Inspections are conducted Monday to Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. (excluding statutory holidays). A Toronto Building Inspector will contact you on the date you identify for the inspection, to schedule the visit for the same day, or the following day. A full scale, coloured print of the permit drawings must be available on site upon the inspector’s request. All information, records, drawings or specifications issued as part of the permit must be available on site for each inspection.

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]

Additionally, inspectors may have to visit your building site several times to conduct the following inspections:

For electrical work:
Tests on electrical wiring shall conform to the Electrical Code or Toronto Transportation Specifications. Tests on electrical equipment shall conform to the appropriate specifications covering the work. The Contractor shall supply all labour, equipment, and material required to carry out all test specified in the contract. All equipment requiring the submission of shop drawings, as detailed in Section 4.0, is subject to inspection by Toronto Transportation or its designate, prior to shipping of the equipment. The inspection shall take place at the manufacturer's factory or at the supplier's place of business. The Contractor shall inform the Contract Administrator of when the equipment fabrication is approximately 80% and 100% complete and shall make suitable arrangements for any required inspection.

All underground work (ducts, handwells, pole bases, controller bases, etc.) must be inspected by Toronto Transportation before the above-ground installation can proceed. The contractor will notify Toronto Transportation in advance of underground work and in advance of re-instatement.

[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/918c-ecs-specs-tcspecs-section-801-100-construction-spec-for-electrical-work-general.pdf]

An officer, other employee, or agent of the City may enter on a property at any reasonable time for the purpose of carrying out an inspection to determine whether or not the following are being complied with:

* This article;
* A direction or order of the City made under this article or the City of Toronto Act, 2006;
* An order made by a court under section 372 of the City of Toronto Act, 2006

A person carrying out an inspection may require the production for inspection of documents or things relevant to the inspection, inspect and remove documents or things relevant to the inspection for the purpose of making copies or extracts, require information from any person concerning a matter related to the inspection, and alone, or in conjunction with a person possessing special or expert knowledge, make examinations or take tests, samples, or photographs necessary for the purpose of the inspection.

3. All drawings, reports, and forms, including the completed Application for a Permit to Construct or Demolish, must be provided in a PDF format.

   - Site Plan: Survey or site plan showing property lines, lot area, right-of-way or easements (referenced to a current survey). Location of existing/proposed buildings with overall dimensions and include setback dimensions to property lines and adjacent buildings. Summary of permitted and proposed zoning provisions to include lot area, building area (GFA), coverage, and grade elevations to confirm height. Indicate dimensioned parking areas, driveways, hard & soft landscape treatments, accessory structures (sheds, decks, detached garages, etc).
   - Lot Grading Plan: Submit a plan showing the proposed grading of the lot, designed in a manner that will result in no new instances of ponding occur on existing adjacent properties and the subject property as a result of construction, in conformance with the Lot Grading Criteria for Infill Housing.
   - Floor Plans: Fully dimensioned, for each level showing existing & proposed uses of all spaces, including location of smoke alarms & carbon monoxide detectors and all plumbing fixtures. Provide existing/proposed construction with foundation & exterior wall information, showing interior partitions and structural framing above.
   - Roof Plan: Existing/proposed roof layout showing roof structure, skylights, roof slopes, hips/valleys/peaks and ventilation.
   - Truss Drawings and Floor Joist Plan: Where Engineered roof trusses or floor systems are proposed.
   - Elevations: Exterior finishes with roof slopes, window/door type, locations & sizes including height of sills above floor level. Provide area of exposed building face, percentage/area of unprotected openings and required limiting distance(s). Show exterior decks/landings, stairs, guards/handrails. Provide overall building height dimension.
   - Sections: Cross section(s) to show existing/proposed building construction and specifications of all floor, wall, & roof assemblies. Provide footing & foundation wall details including height of exterior grade above basement floor. Show floor to floor, floor to ceiling and overall building heights. Detail stairs, landings, guards & handrails.
   - Construction Details and Notes: Building materials & specifications of all wall, floor, and roof assemblies with typical wall section and typical roof detail. Provide guard details including connection detail.
6. Required Forms:
   - Building permit application form required for all submissions
   - Application to Construct or Demolish Form
   - Energy Efficiency Design Summary – Part 9 Residential
   - Compliance using prescriptive method: Prescriptive Energy Efficiency Design Summary Form

prompt: What documents do I need to submit with a building permit application?
answer:
When you apply for a building permit you must submit a complete set of **application forms** and the **drawings and supporting documents** that describe the work you plan to do. The City’s guidance lists the following items as the core documents that are normally required:

| Document | Why it’s required (according to the City) |
|----------|-------------------------------------------|

| **Site plan** (showing the property boundary, existing and proposed structures, easements, setbacks, utility locations, etc.) | Site‑plan information is listed as one of the “required forms, drawings and, if required, site plans and grading plans” needed to begin processing the application. [Source: Building Permit Guide – “You must include all of the required forms, drawings and, if required, site plans and grading plans.”] |
| **Floor plans** for each floor level affected by the work | Floor plans are specifically called out as required: “Floor plans are required for each floor level that is affected by the proposed work.” [Source: Building Permit Guide] |
| **Elevations** (all exterior views of the building) | Elevations are required when the exterior of the house will be altered: “Elevations show all exterior views of a building… may be required for any project that would alter the exterior of your house.” [Source: Building Permit Guide] |
| **Cross‑section drawings** (cut‑away view from footings to roof) | Cross sections are listed as needed to show building materials and how they relate: “A cross section is required to show the building materials and how they relate each other.” [Source: Building Permit Guide] |
| **Roof plan** (existing and new roof framing, truss layout, etc.) | Roof plans are required for roof framing or engineered trusses: “Existing and new roof and ceiling framing must be indicated on the plans… truss layout and designs are required to be submitted with the building permit.” [Source: Building Permit Guide] |
| **Structural drawings** (foundation, footing, framing details) | Structural details are part of the set of “architectural, structural, shoring, mechanical and electrical drawings” that must be grouped by permit type for electronic submission. [Source: File Names for Electronic Documents] |
| **Mechanical / HVAC design** (heating, ventilation, air‑conditioning calculations and drawings) | HVAC design is required for any new mechanical system: “A Heating/Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) design is required for all new mechanical systems serving each dwelling unit.” [Source: Building Permit Guide] |

**How to submit them**

* Upload all required electronic PDFs (application form, all drawings, calculations, specifications) to the Online Services portal or deliver them on a rewritable DVD/USB drive. [Source: Online Services Application Submission User Guide]  
* Include the full‑scale paper reference set of drawings on site for the inspector. [Source: Electronic Submission FAQs]  

If you are unsure whether a particular document is needed for your specific project, the “More Information” links beside each document in the online portal will tell you whether it is required for your proposal. [Source: Online Services Application Submission User Guide]

prompt: How much does a residential building permit cost in Toronto?
answer:
The cost of a residential building permit in Toronto is not a single fixed amount – it is calculated from the size of the work you are proposing and is subject to a few baseline fees.

| Fee | How it is calculated | Example amount |
|-----|----------------------|----------------|
| **Minimum service fee** | Charged on every permit application (unless another fee applies) | **$198.59** per service【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/9678-1184441-c.pdf】 |
| **Residential‑occupancy fee (Group C)** | Charged for the plan‑review and inspection work based on the floor‑area of the residential space | **$17.16 per m²** of floor area【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/9678-1184441-c.pdf】 |
| **Residential‑unit fee (Group C)** | Charged for each new residential unit that the permit creates | **$52.08 per new residential unit**【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/9678-1184441-c.pdf】 |
| **Conditional permit fee** (optional) | 10 % of the total permit fee if you request a conditional permit (adds application intake, plan‑review and inspection activities) | **10 % of the total permit fee**【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/9678-1184441-c.pdf】 |

### What this means for you
1. **Start with the minimum fee** – every residential permit will cost at least **$198.59**.  
2. **Add the floor‑area charge** – multiply the total square metres of the residential floor area by **$17.16**.  
3. **Add the unit charge** – if the permit creates new dwelling units, add **$52.08 for each unit**.  
4. **Optional conditional‑permit surcharge** – if you apply for a conditional permit, add 10 % of the total of the above fees.

**Example** – a new 100 m² single‑family addition that creates one new unit would be calculated as:  

- Minimum fee: $198.59  
- Floor‑area charge: 100 m² × $17.16 = $1,716.00  
- Unit charge: 1 × $52.08 = $52.08  

**Total (before any conditional‑permit surcharge):** **$1,966.67**  

If a conditional permit is requested, add 10 % of $1,966.67 → **$196.67**, for a grand total of **$2,163.34**.

---

**Bottom line:** A residential building permit in Toronto is based on a **minimum $198.59 fee plus $17.16 per m² of residential floor area and $52.08 per new residential unit**, with additional optional surcharges (e.g., 10 % conditional‑permit fee). The exact amount will vary depending on the size and scope of your project.

prompt: What is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto?
answer:
**Applying for a Building Permit in Toronto – Step‑by‑Step**

1. **Prepare your application**  
   • Review the *Building Permit Application Guides* to see which forms, drawings and supporting documents you need (zoning declaration, tree declaration, signed plans, etc.).  
   • Drawings must be high‑quality PDFs (flattened, single file) and, when required, be prepared by a qualified designer (BCIN, OAA or PEO).  
   • Gather any additional paperwork that the City may require for your project type.  
   *[Source: BuildSafeTO – “Steps in the Permit Application Process”]*  

2. **Submit the application**  
   • Email *​bldapplications@toronto.ca* **or** use the **Toronto Building Intake Portal** online.  
   • Include all required documents and the appropriate fees (initial fees are paid by phone once the submission is deemed sufficient).  
   *[Source: BuildSafeTO – “Steps in the Permit Application Process”]*  

3. **Initial review (within 1 business day)**  
   • City staff check whether the submission is **sufficient** to start a formal review.  
   • You receive a **Submission Status Letter** by e‑mail:  
     – **Sufficient** → you are asked to pay the initial fees and a Plan Examiner is assigned.  
     – **Insufficient** → the letter lists the missing items you must provide before a review can begin.  
   *[Source: BuildSafeTO – “Steps in the Permit Application Process”]*  

4. **Plan Review Process** (conducted by the assigned examiners)  

   **a. Zoning Review** – The Zoning Examiner confirms compliance with the Zoning By‑law (uses, size, setbacks, height, parking, etc.) and other applicable laws (Conservation Authorities Act, Planning Act, Environmental Protection Act, Ontario Heritage Act). If the project does not meet the By‑law, you may need a minor variance from the Committee of Adjustment.  
   *[Source: Plan Review Process – “Zoning Review”]*  

   **b. Building Code Review** – A Building Code Examiner checks the plans against the Ontario Building Code for health & safety, fire protection, structural adequacy, materials, plumbing and mechanical systems.  
   *[Source: Plan Review Process – “Building Code Review”]*  

   **c. Mechanical Plans Examination** (if applicable) – Review of HVAC, plumbing, drainage and private sewage system requirements.  
   *[Source: Plan Review Process – “Mechanical Plans Examination”]*  

   **d. Fire Prevention Examination** (for certain multi‑family, commercial, industrial or institutional projects) – Ensures fire‑protection systems meet the Ontario Fire Code.  
   *[Source: Plan Review Process – “Fire Prevention Examination”]*  

5. **Receive the review results**  
   • If the plans comply with all requirements, the application is **approved** and a building permit is issued electronically.  
   • If there are deficiencies, you receive a notice describing why the project does not comply and what additional information or revisions are needed.  
   *[Source: Plan Review Process – “Receive results of the review process”]*  

6. **Pay any remaining fees**  
   • After approval you will be notified of any additional permit fees; payment must be completed before the permit is released.  

7. **Begin work and schedule inspections**  
   • Once the electronic permit is received, you may start construction.  
   • Request mandatory inspections (e.g., introductory, progress, and final inspection) through the **Toronto Building Inspection Requests** web app. The final inspection must be scheduled to close the permit.  
   *[Source: BuildSafeTO – “You will be required to schedule a final inspection upon completion of the project to close the permit.”]*  

8. **Tips to avoid delays**  
   • Apply early and ensure the submission is complete (zoning and tree declarations are common omissions).  
   • Use qualified designers when required and submit properly formatted, high‑quality PDFs.  
   • Respond promptly to any examiner’s notice and submit revised drawings as a single PDF with revision bubbles.  
   *[Source: BuildSafeTO – “Tips for Submitting a Building Permit Application”]*  

**In summary:** Prepare a complete, code‑compliant application; submit it online or by email; obtain a “sufficient” status and pay initial fees; undergo zoning and building‑code reviews; address any examiner’s notices; pay final fees; receive the electronic permit; and schedule the required inspections to complete the project.

prompt: How long does it take to get a building permit approved?
answer:
The City of Toronto does not publish a single, fixed number of days for a building‑permit to be approved. The process works in two stages:

* **Initial sufficiency check** – Once you submit a complete application (including all required forms, drawings and fees), city staff will review it within **one business day** to confirm that the submission is sufficient to start a full review. If it is, you receive a Submission Status Letter and are asked to pay the initial fees. [Source: BuildSafeTO – “Steps in the Permit Application Process”]  

* **Full plan review** – After the application is deemed sufficient, a Plan Examiner conducts a detailed review for compliance with the Zoning By‑law, the Ontario Building Code and any other applicable laws (e.g., Heritage, Conservation Authority). The guide does not give a standard turnaround time for this phase; the length of the review depends on the complexity of the project, the completeness of the submission and whether the examiner needs additional information or revisions. [Source: “Plan Review Process” – Zoning Review, Building Code Review, etc.]

Because there is no published overall deadline, the time to approval can vary widely. You can track the status of your permit at any time through the City’s online permit‑status tool. [Source: “Getting your permit” – check the permit status at http://www.toronto.ca/building-permit-status]

prompt: What inspections are required during construction in Toronto?
answer:
During a construction project in Toronto you must arrange **mandatory building‑code inspections at each critical stage of the work**.  

* **Who must request them:** The builder (or property owner) is responsible for contacting Toronto Building and requesting each required inspection once the project begins. ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

* **When they occur:** The Ontario Building Code (Subsection 1.3.5.1) requires notice to the Chief Building Official whenever the building is ready for a mandatory inspection at each critical stage.  The exact stages depend on the type of construction:  

  * **Small buildings** (Part 9 of the Ontario Building Code – houses and small commercial structures) have their own schedule of mandatory inspections.  
  * **Large buildings** (Part 3 of the Ontario Building Code) follow a different schedule of mandatory inspections.  

  The webpages linked from the “When to call for inspections” sections list the specific inspections for each project type. ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

* **What the inspector must be able to see:** For each inspection the inspector must be able to view the work under review.  Any elements that have been covered must be uncovered, and a full‑scale coloured print of the permit drawings must be available on site. ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

* **Final inspection (permit closure):** When the project is complete you must schedule a **final inspection** so the permit can be closed.  Open permits can hinder future real‑estate transactions or future permit applications. ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

* **Partial occupancy of an unfinished building:** If any part of an unfinished building will be occupied before full completion, the structure must meet Ontario Building Code standards and you must submit an **Authority to Occupy** application prior to occupancy. ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

* **Additional inspections (optional):** You may arrange extra inspections through your local inspection office; these may carry an additional fee. ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

* **Hours of operation:** Inspections are conducted Monday‑Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. (excluding statutory holidays). ​[Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-inspections/about-building-inspections/]  

In summary, Toronto requires **mandatory inspections at each critical construction stage (per Part 9 or Part 3 of the Ontario Building Code), a final inspection to close the permit, and—if occupying part of an unfinished building—an Authority to Occupy application**.  Additional or optional inspections can be arranged if needed.

prompt: Do I need a permit to finish my basement in Toronto?
answer:
Yes – most basement‑finishing work in Toronto requires a building permit.  

The City’s Building Permit Guide lists **“basement finishes”** as one of the interior‑renovation items that “generally… require a building permit before beginning construction”【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/9273-Building-Permit-Guide-WEB.pdf】.  

The more detailed “When Do I Need a Building Permit?” list adds that a permit is required if the basement work involves **any structural or material alteration, new or modified heating or plumbing systems, excavation, underpinning, constructing a basement entrance, or adding a second suite**【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/when-do-i-need-a-building-permit/】.  

If the work is **purely cosmetic** – for example, painting, installing flooring, or adding dry‑wall **without changing walls, adding plumbing, or creating a new dwelling unit** – a permit may **not** be required, but you must still comply with the Zoning Bylaw【Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/when-do-i-need-a-building-permit/】.  

**Bottom line:**  
* Most basement‑finishing projects (especially those that involve structural changes, new plumbing/heating, or a new suite) **do need a building permit**.  
* Purely cosmetic finishes that do not alter the structure or services may be exempt, but you should verify the specifics of your project with Toronto Building or consult the “building‑permit‑required” list on the City’s website.

prompt: What is an express building permit and do I qualify?

An Express Building Permit is a fast‑track permit option for **“smaller, less complex projects within a predefined scope”**. Eligibility for an Express Building Permit depends on whether your project:

1. **Is small in size** (e.g., modest additions, minor alterations, certain accessory structures).  
2. **Is less complex** (does not involve major structural changes, large mechanical systems, or significant fire‑safety upgrades).

Because “predefined scope” can vary (the City provides specific lists of projects that qualify), we need a bit more detail about your planned work to determine if it meets the criteria.

prompt: What is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto?

## Steps in the Permit Application Process

2. **Submit your application** and all required documents and forms to bldapplications@toronto.ca or online using the Toronto Building Intake Portal [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

3. **Initial Review (within one business day):** City staff will review the submission to determine whether it is sufficient. You will receive a Submission Status Letter by email that either:
   - **Finds the application sufficient:** The letter will request payment of initial fees (payable by telephone via credit card). City staff will then assign a Plan Examiner to conduct a full review.
   - **Finds the application insufficient:** The letter will contain the additional items required. You must submit those items before a review can start. [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

4. **Plan Review:** Once a sufficient application is received, staff will undertake a thorough Plan Review for Zoning and Building Code compliance [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

5. **Permit Issuance:** Once your application has been reviewed and found to comply with building regulations, and you have paid all required fees, your permit will be issued electronically [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

6. **Begin Work:** Once you have received your permit, you may begin work on your project [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

7. **Final Inspection:** You are required to schedule a final inspection upon completion of the project to close the permit. Inspections may be requested online using the Toronto Building Inspection Requests web app [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

---

## Tips for Submitting an Application

- Confirm all required forms and documents are signed
- Submit high-quality, properly formatted drawings – sketches are not accepted. All drawings must be flattened, combined in a single PDF, and include all necessary details [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/]

prompt: Do I need a permit to finish my basement in Toronto?

prompt: What are the requirements for a laneway suite permit?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, here are the requirements for a laneway suite building permit in Toronto:

## What Qualifies as a Laneway Suite
A laneway suite is a self-contained residential unit located on the same lot as a detached house, semi-detached house or townhouse, and generally located in the rear yard next to a laneway [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/].

## Required Documentation

**Site Plan** must include:
- Survey or site plan showing property lines, lot area, right-of-way or easements
- Location of existing/proposed buildings with overall dimensions and setback dimensions to property lines and adjacent buildings
- Summary of permitted and proposed zoning provisions (lot area, building area, coverage, grade elevations)
- Dimensioned parking areas, driveways, hard & soft landscape treatments, accessory structures [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

**Lot Grading Plan** showing proposed grading designed to prevent new ponding on adjacent properties, in conformance with Lot Grading Criteria for Infill Housing [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

**Floor Plans** - Fully dimensioned for each level showing existing & proposed uses, smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detectors, and plumbing fixtures [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

**Roof Plan** - Showing roof structure, skylights, roof slopes, hips/valleys/peaks and ventilation [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

**Truss Drawings and Floor Joist Plan** - Where engineered roof trusses or floor systems are proposed [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

**Sections** - Cross sections showing building construction, specifications, footing & foundation details, floor/ceiling heights [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/building-permit-application-guides/renovation-and-new-house-guides/new-laneway-suite/]

prompt: What is the process for applying for a building permit in Toronto?
answer:
The process for applying for a building permit in Toronto involves the following steps:

**1. Prepare Your Application**
Prepare your application for your construction or renovation project using the **Building Permit Application Guides**, which outline required documentation, forms, and fees. Ensure your application is complete, including zoning and tree declaration forms, and that drawings are high-quality, properly formatted (flattened, combined in a single PDF), and prepared by a qualified professional or the property owner if they have the required drafting skills and BCIN or professional designation [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/].

**2. Submit Your Application**
Submit your application and all required documents and forms to **bldapplications@toronto.ca** or online using the **Toronto Building Intake Portal** [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/].

**3. Initial Sufficiency Review**
City staff will review the submission within one business day to determine if it is sufficient to make an application. You will receive a Submission Status Letter by email that either:
- Finds the application is sufficient and requests payment of initial fees (payable by telephone via credit card), after which a Plan Examiner is assigned, or
- Finds the application is insufficient and lists additional items required before review can start [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/].

**4. Plan Review Process**
Once the application is deemed sufficient and fees are paid, staff conduct a thorough review including:
- **Zoning Review**: Checking compliance with the Zoning By-law regarding land use, building size, location, and height. If you cannot comply, you may apply to the Committee of Adjustment for a minor variance [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/].
- **Building Code Review**: Review by a Building Code Examiner for compliance with the Ontario Building Code (health, safety, fire protection, structural sufficiency, materials, plumbing, and mechanical systems) [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/].
- **Mechanical Plans Examination**: If applicable, review of HVAC, plumbing, drainage, and sewage systems [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/].
- **Fire Prevention Examination**: For certain multi-family, commercial, industrial, and institutional applications with fire protection systems [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/].

If compliance issues are found, you will receive an Examiner's Notice documenting why the project does not comply. You must submit additional information via the File Submission Hub (for drawings) or email (for supporting documentation), ensuring revised drawings include revision bubbles and are submitted as a single PDF [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/after-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/plan-review-process/].

**5. Permit Issuance**
Once your application complies with building regulations and all required fees are paid, your permit will be issued electronically. If additional fees are required, you will be notified by email to make payment before issuance [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/].

**6. Construction and Inspections**
Once you receive your permit, you may begin work. You must schedule mandatory inspections at prescribed stages throughout construction using the Toronto Building Inspection Requests web app. For new buildings, an As-Built Survey showing setbacks and first floor elevation must be submitted to the Building Inspector prior to starting construction of the first floor walls [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/98ad-Good_Neighbour_Guide_Digital-shrunk.pdf]. Upon project completion, you must schedule a final inspection to close the permit [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/buildsafeto-learn-about-building-permits/].

answer:

*   Structural or material alterations
*   Installing or modifying heating and/or plumbing systems
*   Excavating and/or constructing foundations
*   Basement underpinning
*   Constructing a basement entrance
*   Adding a second suite (accessory apartment) [Source: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/building-construction/building-permit/before-you-apply-for-a-building-permit/when-do-i-need-a-building-permit/]
